title: MaxFlow-MinCut Duality, Police Chase & König's Vertex Cover

questions.prompt: For a cut $(S, T)$ with $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, which edges contribute to the cut capacity $C(S,T)$?
options: All edges with one endpoint in each of $S$ and $T$.
Only edges directed from $S$ to $T$.
Only edges directed from $T$ to $S$.
Only edges fully inside $S$.
questions.explanation: Only forward edges ($S \to T$) count. Edges from $T \to S$ have weight 0 with respect to the cut and are completely ignored — the classic exam trap.

questions.prompt: Network edges: $s\to A$ (10), $s\to B$ (5), $A\to B$ (4), $A\to t$ (8), $B\to t$ (7). Consider the cut $S=\{s,A\}$, $T=\{B,t\}$. What is $C(S,T)$? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: Forward edges crossing $S\to T$: $s\to B$ (5), $A\to B$ (4), $A\to t$ (8). Sum $= 5+4+8 = 17$. The edge $s\to A$ lies inside $S$, and $B\to t$ lies inside $T$, so neither counts.

questions.prompt: Same network: $s\to A$ (10), $s\to B$ (5), $A\to B$ (4), $A\to t$ (8), $B\to t$ (7). What is the maximum flow value from $s$ to $t$? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: Cut $\{s,A,B\}$ vs $\{t\}$ has capacity $8+7=15$; cut $\{s\}$ has capacity $15$. The min cut is $15$. A flow of $15$ is achievable: $A\to t$ carries $8$, and into $B$ we send $s\to B=5$ plus $A\to B=2$ (total $7$) which exits via $B\to t=7$. So max flow $= 15$.

questions.prompt: Which statements about flow/cut duality are TRUE?
options: Weak duality: for any feasible flow $f$ and any cut $(S,T)$, $|f| \le C(S,T)$.
Strong duality (Max-Flow Min-Cut): $\max|f| = \min_{(S,T)} C(S,T)$.
The minimum cut is always unique.
All forward edges of a minimum cut are saturated at maximum flow.
questions.explanation: Weak and strong duality (A, B) hold, and every forward edge of a min cut must be saturated in a max flow (D). Minimum cuts are NOT always unique (C false) — many networks admit several min cuts of equal capacity.

questions.prompt: After computing a maximum flow, how do you recover a minimum cut in $O(V+E)$?
options: Sort the vertices by degree.
Run BFS/DFS from $s$ in the residual graph using only edges with remaining residual capacity $> 0$; the vertices reached form $S$, the cut edges are original edges $u\in S, v\in T$.
Take all edges incident to $t$.
Re-run the max-flow algorithm from $t$.
questions.explanation: The set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the final residual graph defines the source side $S$ of a minimum cut; original edges crossing from $S$ to $T$ are exactly the saturated min-cut edges.

questions.prompt: In a bipartite graph whose maximum matching has size $5$, what is the size of a minimum vertex cover? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: By König's theorem, in any bipartite graph the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover. So the answer is $5$.

questions.prompt: König's theorem (max matching = min vertex cover) holds for:
options: All graphs.
Bipartite graphs only.
Trees only.
Complete graphs only.
questions.explanation: König's theorem holds specifically for bipartite graphs. In general graphs the two quantities can differ, and minimum vertex cover is NP-hard.

questions.prompt: In the bipartite matching flow network (source $\to$ left $\to$ right $\to$ sink), after computing max flow you run BFS from the source in the residual graph, obtaining reachable set $Z$. Which rules give a minimum vertex cover?
options: Choose left vertices NOT reachable from the source ($L \setminus Z$).
Choose right vertices that ARE reachable from the source ($R \cap Z$).
Choose left vertices that ARE reachable from the source.
Choose right vertices that are NOT reachable from the source.
questions.explanation: The standard recovery: take unreachable left vertices and reachable right vertices. This set has size equal to the max matching/min cut and covers every edge, by the argument that an infinite-capacity left-to-right edge forces reachability to propagate.

questions.prompt: An undirected city graph has streets $1{-}2, 1{-}3, 2{-}4, 3{-}4$. To disconnect intersection $1$ from intersection $4$ you must barricade streets (each barricaded street costs 1). What is the minimum number of streets to barricade? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: Model each undirected street as capacity 1 in both directions. The min cut has capacity 2 (the four options: cut $\{1\}$ gives 2 edges; cut $\{1,2\}$ gives edges $1{-}3$ and $2{-}4$ = 2). So 2 streets must be barricaded, e.g. $1{-}2$ and $3{-}4$.

questions.prompt: Why are edges directed from $T$ to $S$ given weight 0 when computing $C(S,T)$?
options: Because they do not exist in the original network.
Because a cut only severs the source side from the sink side in the forward direction; $T\to S$ edges do not help carry flow from $s$ to $t$ across the cut and so are excluded by definition.
Because their capacities are always negative.
Because the algorithm deletes them.
questions.explanation: Cut capacity measures the total capacity that can carry flow from the $s$-side to the $t$-side. Backward edges ($T\to S$) point the 'wrong way' and are ignored in the sum by definition — a frequent source of off-by-many errors in hand calculations.

questions.prompt: In a max-flow that has been computed, the residual graph has residual-capacity-positive paths from $s$ reaching vertices $\{s, a, b\}$ but not $c$ or $t$. The original edges crossing from $\{s,a,b\}$ to $\{c,t\}$ have capacities $4, 3, 6$. What is the value of the maximum flow? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: The reachable set defines a minimum cut, and the crossing forward edges are saturated, so the max-flow value equals the cut capacity $4+3+6 = 13$.

questions.prompt: The Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem states that the maximum flow value equals:
options: The number of edges in the network.
The capacity of a minimum $s$-$t$ cut.
The number of augmenting paths ever used.
The maximum edge capacity.
questions.explanation: Max-flow = min-cut: the largest flow equals the smallest cut capacity. This strong duality is the backbone of flow theory and unlocks reductions like König's theorem.

questions.prompt: Which statements about minimum cuts are TRUE?
options: Every forward edge of the min cut is saturated at max flow.
There can be more than one minimum cut in a network.
The set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the final residual graph is the source side of a min cut.
A min cut must consist of exactly one edge.
questions.explanation: Saturation, non-uniqueness, and the residual-reachability characterization are all true (A, B, C). A min cut can have any number of edges depending on the network (D false).

questions.prompt: Bipartite graph: left $\{A,B,C\}$, right $\{X,Y,Z\}$, edges $A{-}X, A{-}Y, B{-}X, B{-}Z, C{-}Y$. What is the size of a maximum matching? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: $A{-}X$, $B{-}Z$, $C{-}Y$ form a perfect matching of size 3, matching all left vertices. Since there are only 3 left vertices, 3 is the maximum.

questions.prompt: By Menger's theorem / max-flow min-cut, the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths equals:
options: The number of vertices on a shortest path.
The minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects $s$ from $t$ (the edge-connectivity).
The maximum degree in the graph.
The number of edges in the graph.
questions.explanation: With unit capacities, max flow = minimum number of edges to cut = max edge-disjoint paths. This is the edge version of Menger's theorem, and it is exactly the Police Chase / CSES problem.
